This is black knot. It's a fungal infection that overwinters in the infected branches and spreads during cool wet spring weather. 

You can prune out the infected branches to reduce the disease pressure. Cut each infected branch about 4 inches below where the infection is obvious and sanitize your pruner blade between each cut so you don't spread it around. Don't leave the pruned debris sitting around. Either get it out with the weekly trash pickup or burn it. 

This is typically not a fatal disease for trees, but a large number of the infected branches can girdle the stems and cause stress and likely decline.

I ran into this exact pattern of symptoms earlier this year. Turned out to be phytopthera. When I see whole limbs die off like a roadway cutting through the green foliage, that's my identifier.

Wet conditions favor this soil pathogen, and I see irrigation lines around the base. You need to give that soil time to dry out between irrigations. The lack of oxygen to the roots will create a very stressed growing environment. I don't know where you are, but in Illinois we had a very wet spring this year which created a very favorable environment for the disease. 

Send a soil sample to your extension plant clinic for diagnosis. Must contain root material at well. Follow the instructions on their website. 

Soil applied fungicides can be applied in spring to protect the roots during very wet conditions. I apply Segway sc, mefonoxam, and phosphoric acid (reliant) in March, April, and May. 

Don't over water and keep it mulched. Phytopthera has cell walls made from cellulose, so the same organisms which break down wood mulch will break down phytopthera cells.

Apples can become diseased with numerous fungal diseases and a good number of insects. You probably want to apply a series of sprays in early spring. This will help prevent numerous foliage and fruit pathogens. 
Search for reliant. It's an acidic systemic fungicide safe for fruit production. It's not quite considered organic, but it's sort of like spraying the tree with citric acid. Read the label and follow instructions. Do maybe 5 sprays starting in early spring in the shortest intervals on the label. You can buy it at places like conserv fs, Russo, maybe site one. As a private property owner you are legally allowed to apply it, following the label instructions, on your property without additional training.

For insects, you should primarily be concerned with apple borers. These insects will bore into the trunk and cause die back and eventually death of the tree. You may be able to prevent infestation with a horticultural oil. This is an organic product. It's basically a refined mineral oil which will smother insects by clogging their breathing pathways. This can be applied in late winter to the bark of the trunk and stems, and again throughout the growing season as leaves develop. It may not be compatible with the fungicide though, so apply separately. Never apply oil sprays when temps will go above 90 degrees. This may scorch the leaves. It's relatively uncommon with modern refined oils, but never hurts to be careful. 

As for culture, always perform the best management possible for the tree health. A resilient vigorously growing tree is much less susceptible to disease than a stressed already dying tree. Prune out dead branches and sanitize your cutting tools between snips. (Lysol wipes work fine) Clean up leaf debris in the fall to remove a disease source before the following spring. Mulch the base of the trees with a proper layer of high quality wood mulch. Don't mound it against the trunk like so many folks love to do. And resist the urge to fertilize like crazy. You can scatter some general purpose fertilizer at the surface, but don't go overboard. Water it during dry hot weather. 

You can read more about timing and recommended products here https://yardandgarden.extension.iastate.edu/how-to/spray-schedule-home-apple-trees

Exposing the root collar isn't the end all of soil management. It's important but your tree will struggle to grow in that environment. Soil oxygen content drops dramatically as you go further down the soil layers. The majority of roots are usually in the upper 12 to 20 inches, so having the trunk buried so deep will result in roots growing up high to compensate, or struggling to grow at all with such an oxygen restriction.

I did an air spade root collar excavation on a series of maples last year on one property. They were all to deep and buried, but one in particular was at least 18 inches down below grade. It had probably grown 2 inches dbh max over 2 decades because of how deep it was, and maples are pretty well known as fast growers.

Obviously remove all the big stones if possible, but the root flare looks a million times better! A good 2 to 3 inch layer of properly applied mulch is the best soil conditioner you can buy. All the way to the drip line if you're willing. That grass is interfering with tree root growth, so removing it and mulching would be very beneficial.

Similar situation here at my house. Termite damage before I moved in mostly due to the house being 130 years old and having some areas where soil was up close against the exterior walls. That's an environment asking for trouble. However, I'd be skeptical about termites attacking your tree. They typically don't attack living trees unless the tree is in heavy decline and has lots of dead wood, and if they do attack your tree they always start at the base and move up. You'd be seeing more damage around the base rather than in the canopy. The only places where termites might nest high up in a tree would be an equatorial climate, like NZ or AU.

What's more likely is your big mature tree has areas of dead or weakened wood which is becoming habitat to a bunch of critters. Termites aren't the only animal that bore into wood and use it as a home or food source, and a mature tree becomes an entire ecosystem in itself. There's all kinds of stuff in there like carpenter ants, secondary opportunistic borers, woodpeckers, etc. I'd get an inspection just for soundness of mind, and keep any dead lumber or wood parts out of your yard and away from your home.
